definition: Every point where an attacker can interact with a system: inputs, APIs, credentials, network services.
A person or group with the intent and capability to attack a system.
A structured description of assets, trust boundaries and the threats that cross them.
A weakness that could be exploited to violate a security property.
Concrete technique or code that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
A vulnerability with no vendor fix available at the time it is used or disclosed.
A unique identifier assigned to a publicly disclosed vulnerability.
A scoring system that expresses the severity of a vulnerability.
A taxonomy of software weakness types, such as SQL injection.
A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques observed in the wild.
Layering independent controls so a single failure does not compromise the system.
Giving every identity only the permissions it needs for its task.
A line where data or control crosses between different privilege levels.
Proving an identity is who it claims to be.
Deciding what an authenticated identity may do.
Authentication that requires two or more independent factors.
An attack where the attacker forces a victim to use a known session identifier.
Cross-site request forgery: a site causes a logged-in user's browser to perform an unwanted action.
Cross-site scripting: injecting script into pages viewed by other users.
Inserting SQL syntax through user input so the database executes unintended statements.
Server-side request forgery: making the server request an attacker-chosen destination.
Insecure direct object reference: reaching another user's object because authorization is missing.
Using ../ sequences to escape an intended directory.
Passing untrusted input to a shell so it is executed as a command.
Converting untrusted bytes back into objects, which can execute code in unsafe formats.
Content Security Policy: a response header that restricts which resources a page may load.
HTTP Strict Transport Security: tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a site.
Transport Layer Security: protocol that encrypts and authenticates network traffic.
Restricting which certificates a client will accept for a service.
A one-way function that maps data to a fixed-size digest.
Random data added to a password before hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes.
A deliberately slow function that turns a password into a key or hash.
A keyed hash used to verify integrity and authenticity of a message.
A cryptographic proof that a message came from the holder of a private key.
A value used once to prevent replay or reuse in cryptographic protocols.
A measure of unpredictability, usually in bits, used to judge secret strength.
An HTTP response header that instructs the browser to enforce a protection.
Web application firewall: inspects and filters HTTP traffic against known attack patterns.
Security information and event management: aggregates logs and alerts on patterns.
Endpoint detection and response: monitors endpoints for malicious behavior.
Intrusion detection system: alerts on suspicious network or host activity.
Intrusion prevention system: blocks traffic it classifies as malicious.
A decoy system designed to attract and observe attackers.
Deception that tricks a person into revealing credentials or running malware.
Phishing tailored to a specific person or team using researched details.
Manipulating people into breaking security procedures.
The structured process for detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from an incident.
Collecting and analyzing evidence from systems in a way that preserves integrity.
Documentation of who handled evidence, when, and how it was protected.
Indicator of compromise: an observable artifact suggesting an intrusion.
Tactics, techniques and procedures: how an adversary operates.
Intelligence gathered from public sources, used lawfully and ethically.
Reporting a vulnerability privately and coordinating publication with the vendor.
A program that pays researchers for reporting vulnerabilities within scope.
The systems and techniques an engagement is authorized to touch.
The written agreement on targets, timing, techniques and escalation.
Reducing the attack surface of a system through configuration and removal of unnecessary features.
The process of tracking and applying security updates.
Physically isolating a system from untrusted networks.
An isolated environment that limits what code can access.
Gaining rights beyond those initially granted.
Moving from one compromised host to another inside a network.
Mechanisms that keep an attacker's access across reboots and credential changes.
